after.text:
In this article, aiming to evaluate ζ (−m) as a value of the analytically continued
function ζ (s) in the most elementary, yet rigorous, way possible, we present an
alternative approach. We introduce and investigate a q-analogue of the Riemann zeta
function. As becomes clear in the course of our study, this function serves very well
for the purpose of not only computing ζ (−m), but also providing a q-analogue which
is valid for all s ∈ C; in other words, in the classical limit q → 1 the value approaches
to ζ (s) for all s.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Finite-difference annihilation isolates the Bernoulli coefficient in the classical limit
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Theorem 1 rewrites the negative-integer formula as a finite alternating binomial sum, inserts the Bernoulli generating series, and uses a derivative/finite-difference identity that kills every intermediate degree. neighboring_unit_entries.title: Pointwise convergence to zeta can coexist with severe finite-sum instability near a zero
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Theorem 2 asserts convergence for every complex s except the pole. related_synthesis_entries.limit: This relation is proved for the source's specific q-zeta and Bernoulli normalization and should not be generalized to arbitrary q-analogues without checking their singular and sign conventions.

unit_result_entry.title: Repeated integration by parts moves incomplete-beta parameters and exposes an arbitrarily extendable half-plane
unit_result_entry.why_material: The incomplete beta integral is recursively decomposed into finitely many boundary terms plus a shifted remainder. Applying this to each Fourier mode extends the expression to Re(s)>2-M, so increasing M now genuinely enlarges the continuation domain.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Fourier expansion converts the blocked periodic remainder into uniformly controlled incomplete-beta modes
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Replacing the periodic Bernoulli polynomial by its uniformly convergent Fourier series permits interchange of sum and integral. The substitution q^x=u then packages each Fourier mode as an incomplete beta integral with a uniform-in-mode bound, creating a continuation route unavailable in the original x-representation.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: The q-limit reproduces the classical Euler-Maclaurin continuation term by term
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: After taking the elementary q-to-1 limits, Fourier identities turn the beta-mode boundary terms into Bernoulli corrections and the surviving remainder into the periodic-Bernoulli integral. The resulting expression is exactly the classical formula for zeta, and arbitrary M covers the entire plane except the pole.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: The classical Euler-Maclaurin proof succeeds because increasing remainder order moves the convergence boundary, whereas the direct q-version is pinned by q^{x(s-1)}. Fourier decomposition and the substitution q^x=u create beta integrals whose integration-by-parts order does move that boundary, after which the q-limit reconstructs the original classical continuation.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The transfer depends on uniform Fourier convergence, mode bounds, and formula-sensitive limit interchange established in this source; it is not a generic license to replace every blocked remainder by a Fourier expansion.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: The proof establishes pointwise classical convergence, yet the near-zero examples show that enormous truncations can remain badly conditioned before eventual convergence. A valid deformation can therefore be conceptually exact while computationally ineffective in sensitive regions.
